title: Yoga (revisited)
hook: a brown line worn across a green lawn, and Vyasa's wheel of thoughts and traces

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yoga's Ishvara: the purusha never caught, teacher of even the earliest teachers, whose word is Om.

Outside a library, a brown line runs across the lawn. Nobody planned it. There's a paved walkway around the corner, but someone once cut across the grass to save a few steps. Then someone else followed, because the grass was a little flatter there. Then everyone after. Now the line is bare dirt, and new feet take it without deciding to. The path made the walking, and the walking made the path. Vyasa's commentary on Yoga describes the mind working just like that lawn, and gives the loop a name.
screen: `A LINE ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `NOBODY PLANNED IT.` → `THE WALKING MAKES THE PATH.`

segments.voice: The name is samskara. In the Yoga Sutras it means the trace an experience leaves behind in the mind, like a footprint in grass. Patanjali's word for the mind's movements is vritti, a turning. Vyasa, commenting on the early sutras, ties the two together in a loop. Turnings leave traces, he says, and traces give rise to turnings again. And so the wheel of turnings and traces keeps going round, without pause. That's the lawn. A worry shows up, it leaves a groove, and the groove makes the next worry easier to have. In Yoga's account, that isn't a moral failing. It's how minds work. So what can be done about a path worn that deep? You can't argue a lawn out of its line. Here's the hopeful turn, near the end of the first chapter. Patanjali says that a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces. He means deep insight, not one good afternoon. But the principle carries: what wore the old path can wear a new one. Read in a small way, every time attention comes back to the breath, every time a sharp reply gets a second look, that's a footstep somewhere new. That's why Yoga cares so much about doing things again and again. Not because repetition is a virtue in itself, but because that's how a lawn changes. One more thing. Samskara has other homes in Hindu life. The same word names the rites that mark a life, from naming a child to a wedding. In Yoga, it means something quieter: the grooves underneath the next thought.
screen: `TURNINGS LEAVE TRACES.` · `TRACES MAKE TURNINGS.` · `A NEW TRACE BLOCKS THE OLD.` · `EVERY RETURN IS A FOOTSTEP.`

segments.voice: Rest attention on the breath in the belly, and let the mind wander down its old lines, the usual worry, the usual plan. Each time you notice, come back, and count, if anything, the returns rather than the wanderings: each one is a step across new grass. If you pray, you can let each return be a small offering.
Yoga. Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces and traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can block the old ones. Samskara is the trace.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Every return to the breath is a footstep on new grass. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn Vyasa's picture of the wheel of turnings and traces, and teachers use it to explain why steady, repeated practice matters: each return of attention lays down a new trace.
